### Background

Medical errors are a serious public health problem. The Institute of Medicine estimates that approximately 98,000 people die annually in the United States due to medical errors [1]. However, medical errors are not currently reported to the public. The main argument against public reporting is that it will deter patients from seeking care. This study aimed to determine whether patients are willing to pay to publicly report medical errors and whether willingness to pay is associated with patients’ sociodemographic characteristics.

### Methods

A discrete choice experiment was conducted to assess willingness to pay for publicly reporting medical errors. Participants were recruited from the University of Florida campus and surrounding areas. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 choice sets and asked to choose between two options: a) a healthcare system with a publicly reported medical error rate and a lower healthcare cost, or b) a healthcare system with no publicly reported medical error rate and a higher healthcare cost. The choice sets varied based on the error rate (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 errors per 100,000 patients), the cost (increasing from $0 to$50), and the type of error (preventable or non-preventable). Willingness to pay was calculated as the maximum cost a participant was willing to pay for the healthcare system with publicly reported medical errors. Willingness to pay was regressed on patients’ sociodemographic characteristics using a generalized linear model.

### Results

The study included 150 participants. The average willingness to pay was $11.00 (SD =$10.00). Patients were willing to pay more for publicly reported preventable medical errors than for non-preventable medical errors (p < 0.001). Patients’ willingness to pay was not significantly associated with sociodemographic characteristics.

### Conclusion

Patients are willing to pay to publicly report medical errors, and willingness to pay is higher for preventable medical errors. Further research is needed to determine whether patients’ willingness to pay for publicly reported medical errors will translate into a reduction in medical errors.
